p.src: Now the story tells how Shi Xiu returned and, seeing that the shop had been cleared away, prepared to take his leave and depart. Old Pan said, “Uncle, stay a while. This old man already knows what you are thinking. You did not come home for two nights, and when you returned today and saw that the household utensils had been put away, you decided we must be closing the shop, and so you meant to leave. Even if we did not have such a thriving business—why, even if we closed the shop—I would still keep you here in the family. To tell you the truth, my young daughter was first married to a clerk named Wang in this prefecture. Sadly, he died, and now that the second anniversary of his death has come, we are holding some rites for his soul. That is why we have suspended business for these two days. Tomorrow we have invited monks from Bao’en Monastery to perform the memorial service, and I would like to ask you to take charge of receiving them. This old man is advanced in years and cannot endure staying up at night, so I thought I had better tell you everything plainly.” Shi Xiu said, “Since you put it that way, Father, I shall settle myself again and stay on for a while.” Old Pan said, “From now on, Uncle, harbor no suspicions. Just live here as circumstances allow.” They then drank several cups of wine and ate some vegetarian fare, after which the cups and dishes were cleared away.

p.src: The monk entered and made a deep obeisance to Shi Xiu. Shi Xiu returned the courtesy and said, “Reverend, please sit a while.” Behind him came a Daoist attendant carrying two boxes on a shoulder pole. Shi Xiu called out, “Father, a reverend has come.” Hearing him, Old Pan came out from within. The monk said, “Godfather, why have you not visited our humble monastery for so long?” The old man said, “It is because I opened these shops and have had no time to get away.” The monk then said, “For Clerk Wang’s death anniversary, I have nothing rare to present—only a little dried vermicelli and several packets of capital dates. …” The old man said, “Oh, what need was there? You have put yourself to needless expense, Reverend!” He told Shi Xiu to take the gifts inside. Shi Xiu carried them in himself, ordered tea to be prepared, and invited the monk to drink it at the front of the house.

p.src: Just then the woman came down from upstairs. Not daring to wear full mourning, she had only lightly powdered and adorned herself. She asked, “Uncle, who sent those things?” Shi Xiu said, “A monk who calls Father his godfather brought them.” The woman smiled and said, “That must be my brother in the faith, Preceptor Hai, Pei Ruhai—an honest monk. He is the young master of the Pei family’s silk-thread shop and took holy orders at Bao’en Monastery. Because his master was a disciple of our household and became sworn kin with my father, making Father his godfather, and because Ruhai is two years older than I am, I call him elder brother in the faith. His Dharma name is Master Hai. —Uncle, tonight just listen when he invokes the Buddha and chants the sutras. What a fine voice he has!” Shi Xiu said, “So that is how it is.” But inwardly, he had already begun to suspect something.

p.src: The woman came downstairs to see the monk. Shi Xiu clasped his hands behind his back and followed her out, then peered through the cloth curtain. As soon as the woman came outside, the monk rose, stepped forward, pressed his palms together, and made a deep obeisance. The woman said, “What need was there for this, elder brother? You have put yourself to needless expense!” The monk said, “Worthy sister, it is only a trifling gift of humble things, hardly worth mentioning.” The woman said, “Why do you speak so, elder brother? How could I accept things belonging to a man of religion?” The monk said, “Our humble monastery has newly built a Hall for the Water-and-Land Rite, and I mean to invite you to come and share in its merit. I only fear the warden might take offense.” The woman said, “My unworthy husband is not so petty. When my mother died, I also vowed to have the Blood-Basin Rite performed, and sooner or later I must trouble your honored monastery to fulfill that vow.” The monk said, “That is a matter among our own family. Why speak so formally? Whatever you instruct Ruhai to do, this humble monk will see it done.” The woman said, “Elder brother, it will be enough if you recite a few more scrolls of scripture for my mother.” Just then a maid came from within carrying tea. The woman picked up a cup, wiped its rim with her handkerchief, and presented it to the monk with both hands. As the monk accepted the tea, his two lust-glazed eyes never left the woman’s body. The woman, for her part, looked at the monk with a coy smile. It is said that lust makes boldness reach the heavens, yet neither of them suspected that Shi Xiu was watching through the cloth curtain. Shi Xiu thought secretly to himself, “‘Trust not the uprightness of one who seems upright; beware the heartlessness of one who seems humane.’ Several times I have seen that woman forever directing flirtatious talk at me, but I have always treated her exactly as my own sister-in-law. So it turns out she is no virtuous woman after all. Let her not fall into Shi Xiu’s hands. I just might bring this affair to a reckoning on Yang Xiong’s behalf.”

p.src: By now Shi Xiu was already somewhat suspicious, so he raised the cloth curtain and came out. The thieving bald monk set down his teacup and said, “Please sit down, sir.” The woman interjected, “This gentleman is a sworn brother my husband has newly taken.” The monk, concealing his unease behind a cold manner, asked, “Where is your native place, sir? May I ask your honored surname and given name?” Shi Xiu replied, “My surname is Shi and my given name is Xiu. I am from Jinling. Because I cannot resist meddling in other people’s affairs and risking myself on their behalf, I am called ‘Desperate Third Brother.’ I am a rough fellow and know little of ceremony, so do not take offense, Reverend!” Pei Ruhai said, “Not at all, not at all. This humble monk must go and fetch the other monks for the service.” He took his leave and went out. The woman said, “Come back early, Brother.” The monk answered, “I shall be right back.” After seeing the monk out, the woman went back inside. Shi Xiu remained by the doorway, head bowed, lost in thought. Now, dear reader, listen: of all people in the world, monks are the most fiercely lustful. Why do I say this? Laymen and men who leave the world are alike born of a father’s seed and a mother’s blood; why, then, should monks be deemed the most lustful? Of the five things named in the earlier three volumes—Pan, donkey, Deng, youth, and leisure—it is monks who possess leisure in the greatest measure. Three meals a day they enjoy the fine vegetarian fare and offerings of their lay patrons; they dwell in lofty halls, grand shrines, and monastic quarters; no worldly business troubles them; and as they lie on fine beds and bedding with nothing else to ponder, they think only of this one matter. Take, by way of comparison, a wealthy man: though he may possess every advantage, countless affairs vex him by day, and at night his money and property weigh upon his mind. He does not sleep until the second or third watch, and even with lovely wives and beautiful concubines sharing his bed and pillow, how can he have any amorous pleasure? Then there are the common poor, who struggle and toil the whole day long, yearning from morning for evening, rising in the fifth watch and not sleeping until midnight. Come evening, before going to bed, they first feel inside the rice jar, only to find not a grain left and no money for the morrow. Though their wives may have some beauty, they have not the least inclination for pleasure. Thus they cannot compete with monks, whose minds are free and tranquil and who devote themselves wholly to such business. When the ancients discussed this point, they declared monks formidable indeed. p.src: When the monks upon the altar saw the woman, they unconsciously began waving their hands and stamping their feet. In an instant their Buddha-nature and meditative minds were lost in delusion, and they could no longer rein in the ape of the mind or the horse of desire. Thus are truly virtuous and eminent monks rare in this world. Watching from the side, Shi Xiu gave a cold laugh and said, “What merit can there be in this? As the saying goes, doing good works is not so worthwhile as avoiding sin.” A little later, when the rites had been completed, the monks were invited inside to take their vegetarian meal. Walking behind the other monks, Acarya Hai turned his head and looked at the woman with a broad grin. The woman covered her mouth and smiled as well. The two exchanged glances, conveying their passion with their eyes. Shi Xiu saw it all, and his displeasure rose by half. The monks sat down to eat, first drinking several cups of vegetarian wine. When the meal was brought out, each laid down his offering money. Old Pan said, “Reverend sirs, please eat your fill.” Presently, when they had finished, the monks rose to walk off the meal. After making a circuit, they returned to the service. Shi Xiu felt intensely displeased. Pretending to have a stomachache, he went and lay down behind the plank partition.

p.src: Once the woman’s passion had been stirred, she gave no thought to guarding against being seen. She went to attend to the monks; they performed another round with drums and cymbals, while she prepared tea, refreshments, and fruit. Acarya Hai instructed the monks to apply themselves to reading the scriptures, invoke the Heavenly Kings and perform repentance, prepare the ritual bath and summon the dead, and pay homage to the Three Jewels. The rites for the dead continued until the third watch. Though the other monks grew weary, Acarya Hai became ever more energetic and chanted the scriptures in a loud voice. Watching from beneath the cloth curtain, the woman felt the flames of desire blaze up within her. Unable to restrain her passion, she told her maid Yinghuan to ask Monk Hai to come speak with her. The thieving bald monk hurried over to her. The woman caught hold of his sleeve and said, “Brother, when you come tomorrow to collect the merit money, tell Father about the vow concerning the Blood-Bowl rite. Do not forget.” The monk said, “This humble monk shall remember. Just say you wish to fulfill the vow; it would be well to do so.” The monk added, “That brother-in-law of your household is a most formidable man.” The woman replied, “What does he matter? He is no blood relation.” Acarya Hai said, “In that case, this humble monk can set his mind at ease. I had thought he was the constable’s own brother.” The two flirted and laughed together for a while longer. The monk then went back out to measure out the offerings and send off the dead. Little did they know that Shi Xiu was only feigning sleep behind the plank partition. With his ears pricked, he took it all in. At the fifth watch that night, the service concluded. After seeing off the Buddhas and burning the paper offerings, the monks gave thanks and departed, while the woman went upstairs to sleep. Shi Xiu brooded angrily, “My brother is such a hero—what bitter luck that he has fallen in with this wanton woman!” Swallowing a bellyful of foul anger, he went to sleep in the workshop.

p.src: The next day, Yang Xiong returned home, and none of them mentioned the matter. After the meal, Yang Xiong went out again. Presently Monk Hai appeared, changed into another spotless set of monastic robes, and went straight to Pan's house. When the woman heard that the monk had come, she hurried downstairs, went out to receive him, invited him inside to sit, and ordered tea to be prepared. The woman thanked him, saying, “Last night I put you to much trouble, Brother, yet I have not presented the money for the merit-making service.” Monk Hai said, “It is hardly worth mentioning. I have come especially to tell you, worthy sister, about the vow to perform the Blood-Bowl penitential rite that I mentioned last night. If you wish to fulfill it, the monks at my temple are now chanting scriptures, and only a single memorial petition need be prepared.” The woman said, “Good, good.” She then told her maid to invite her father out to discuss it. Old Pan came out and apologized, “This old man cannot endure much exertion, and last night I was sadly remiss in attending you. Who would have thought that Uncle Shi would be laid low by another stomachache? p.src: These words, handed down by the ancients, speak solely of the retribution of good and evil, which follows as closely as a shadow follows the form. Having cultivated the Six Perfections and all manner of good affinities, one should observe the Three Refuges and Five Precepts. Yet intolerably, some of the black-robed clergy devote themselves to the conduct of dogs and swine, disgracing their forebears in the faith and leaving infamy to later generations. Now this thieving bald priest, Preceptor Hai, had made Old Pan his godfather solely for the woman's sake. But Yang Xiong was always in his way and under his eye, so he had been unable to lay hands on her. Ever since becoming acquainted with the woman, he had merely traded amorous glances with her; nothing had actually happened between them. It was only during that night's service that they finally conveyed their intentions to each other and fixed the appointed day. The thieving bald priest pulled himself together and waited beneath the monastery gate. When he saw the sedan chair arrive, he was beside himself with joy and went forward to welcome it. Old Pan said, “We have put you to a great deal of trouble, Reverend.” The woman alighted from the chair and thanked him. “I am deeply obliged to you, Brother.” Preceptor Hai said, “Not at all, not at all! The other monks and I have been in the Water-and-Land Hall reciting sutras since the fifth watch. We have not rested even now, but have waited for my worthy sister to come and witness the vows. This will earn abundant merit.” He led the woman and her father into the Water-and-Land Hall, where flowers, fruit, incense, candles, and the like had already been arranged. More than ten monks sat there reading sutras. The woman bowed to them all and paid reverence to the Three Jewels. Preceptor Hai led them before Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva to bear witness to the vows and perform repentance. When the memorial had been read through, he burned the paper, invited the other monks to take their vegetarian meal, and ordered his disciples to attend them. Monk Hai then invited his godfather and worthy sister to his quarters for tea. With repeated invitations he led the woman deep into the monks’ quarters, where everything had been prepared beforehand. He called, “Brother, bring the tea!” Two attendants appeared bearing exceedingly fine tea in snow-white pewter cups set upon vermilion saucers. After they had drunk and set down their cups, he invited his worthy sister to sit awhile farther inside. He led them into a small upper chamber, furnished with a gleaming black-lacquered table, several scrolls of calligraphy and paintings by famous masters, and a burner of exquisite incense upon a little table. Old Pan and his daughter sat together on one side of the table, the monk sat opposite, and Ying’er stood beside them. The woman said, “Brother, this truly is a fine retreat for a man of religion—secluded, tranquil, and delightful.” Preceptor Hai replied, “Do not make fun of me, Sister. How could this compare with your noble residence?” Old Pan said, “We have imposed on you all day, Brother. We shall be going home.” But the monk would not hear of it. “It is a rare pleasure to have my godfather here, and you are no strangers. My worthy sister has already sponsored today’s vegetarian feast; how could you leave without eating so much as a bowl of noodles? Brother, bring it in at once!” Before he had finished speaking, two trays were carried in, laden with rare fruits, unusual vegetables, and all manner of vegetarian delicacies that had been stored away for the occasion, until the lacquered table was completely covered. The woman said, “Brother, why go to the trouble of serving wine? We have only come to inconvenience you.” The monk laughed. “It is scarcely a proper reception—merely a small token of my regard.” His fellow monk brought the wine and poured it into their cups. The monk said, “Godfather, you have not visited for a long while. Taste this wine.” After drinking, the old man said, “Fine wine! It has a truly powerful flavor.” The monk said, “The other day a patron’s household taught me this method, and we brewed three or five piculs of rice. Tomorrow I shall send several jars for your son-in-law to drink.” The old man said, “There is no need for that. …” The monk urged them again: “I have nothing with which to repay my worthy sister, so please condescend to drink one cup.” The two young monks took turns pouring wine, and at their urging even Ying’er drank several cups. The woman said, “Enough wine. I cannot drink any more.” The monk said, “It is rare to have my worthy sister here. Please, drink a few more cups.” Old Pan called the sedan-chair bearers inside and gave each of them a cup of wine.

p.src: The monk said, “Help Godfather to a bed so that he may sleep awhile.” He called two fellow monks, who supported the old man between them and took him to sleep in a cool, quiet room. The monk remained behind and urged the woman, “Madam, drink freely—a few more cups.” The woman already had designs of her own, and the wine now stirred her passions. As the old saying goes, “Wine disorders the nature, and lust bewilders the mind.” Once three cups had entered her belly, the woman began to feel hazy and called out noisily, “Brother, why do you keep pressing me to drink?” The monk grinned broadly. “Only because I hold you in such esteem, Madam.” The woman said, “I cannot drink any more.” The monk said, “Come to my room, Madam, and see the Buddha’s tooth.” The woman replied, “That is precisely what I should like to see.” The monk led her upstairs to a room that proved to be Preceptor Hai’s bedchamber, furnished with impeccable neatness. At the sight of it the woman was already half delighted. She said, “You truly have a fine bedchamber, so spotless and tidy.” The monk laughed. “It lacks only a lady.” The woman laughed as well. “Could you not find yourself one?” The monk said, “Where could I find a patroness such as that?” The woman said, “For now, let me see the Buddha’s tooth.” The monk said, “Send Ying’er downstairs, and then I shall bring it out.” The woman said, “Ying’er, go downstairs and see whether the old master has awakened.” Ying’er went downstairs to check on Old Pan, and the monk shut the upstairs door. The woman said, “Brother, why have you shut me in here?” Lust surging through him, the thieving bald priest stepped forward, clasped the woman, and said, “Madam, I adore you beyond measure. p.src: Heedless of the Tathāgata’s sacred law, they could not obey the Buddha’s bequeathed commands. One, emboldened and led astray by lust, cared nothing for how formidable her husband might be; The other, his lecherous heart surging, cared nothing for the abbot’s reproach. This one gasped and groaned, like an ox emerging beneath the shadows of willows; The other spoke in coy, breathless tones, like an oriole warbling among the flowers. One whispered cloud-borne longing and rainy passion into an ear; the other, upon the pillow, swore vows as enduring as mountains and seas. Within the preceptor’s chamber, the place of worship became instead a sanctuary of pleasure; Within the Temple of Requited Grace, this truly was the Pure Land of Utmost Bliss. What a pity that the sweet dew of enlightenment should all at once be spilled amid artful clouds.

p.src: When their bout of love was over, the bald rogue clasped the woman and said, “Since you have set your heart on me, I could die without regret. But though you fulfilled my desire today, we enjoyed only a moment's bliss and could not make merry the whole night; sooner or later this will surely be the death of this poor monk.” The woman replied, “Do not fret. I have already thought of a plan. My husband spends some twenty nights a month sleeping at the prison where he is on duty. I bought Ying'er expressly to have her keep watch by the back gate every day. On any night when my husband is away, I shall have a little incense table carried outside and burn incense upon it as our signal; then you may come without fear. If we fear that we may sleep past the fifth watch and fail to wake, we need only find a mendicant monk who calls the dawn, station him by the back gate, and have him beat his wooden fish loudly and invoke the Buddha at the top of his voice; then you can slip away. If we can hire such a man, he can first keep watch outside and, second, make sure you do not oversleep until dawn.” Hearing this, the monk was overjoyed. “Wonderful! Just do as you have said. I know a mendicant named Daoist Hu here, and I shall instruct him to keep watch for us.” The woman said, “I dare not linger, lest those fellows grow suspicious. I had best hurry home. Only be sure not to miss our appointment.” The woman hastily rearranged her cloudlike hair, repowdered her face, opened the upper-room door, and went downstairs. She had Ying'er wake Master Pan, then hurried out of the monks' quarters. The sedan-chair bearers had eaten their wine and noodles and were already waiting before the temple gate. Preceptor Hai escorted the woman all the way beyond the outer gate. She bade him farewell and mounted her chair, then returned home with Master Pan and Ying'er. No more need be said of that.

p.src: Now Preceptor Hai went to seek out the mendicant who called the dawn. There happened to be a Daoist Hu attached to his quarters, who lived in a small hermitage in the retirement compound behind the temple. Everyone called him Mendicant Hu. Each day he rose at the fifth watch, went about beating his wooden fish to announce the dawn and exhorting people to invoke the Buddha; when day broke, he collected vegetarian food. Monk Hai summoned him to his room, treated him to three cups of fine wine, and then gave Daoist Hu some silver. Daoist Hu rose and said, “Your disciple has rendered no service. p.src: Now it happened that Yang Xiong was due for night duty at the prison that day. Before evening fell, he came home for his bedding and went to sleep at the jail. Ying'er, having received her little signal, could scarcely wait for nightfall. She prepared the incense table and, at dusk, carried it outside the back door, while the woman hid nearby and waited. Around the first watch, a man wearing a headcloth slipped inside. Ying'er asked, “Who is it?” The man made no answer, but removed the headcloth and revealed his shaven crown. Seeing from the side that it was Monk Hai, the woman softly cursed, “You thieving baldhead—you certainly know what to do.” The two embraced and clung to each other as they went upstairs. Ying'er came and carried away the incense table, shut the back door, and went to bed herself. That night the pair were close as glue and lacquer, sweet as sugar and honey, rich as cream and marrow, harmonious as fish in water, and spent the whole night in wanton pleasure. As the old saying goes: “Do not complain that nights of pleasure are too brief; only wish the golden cock would delay its cry of dawn.” The two were sleeping soundly when they heard the clack-clack of a wooden fish and a loud invocation of the Buddha. The monk and the woman awoke with a start. Preceptor Hai put on his clothes, rose, and said, “I must go. We shall meet again tonight.” The woman said, “From now on, whenever the incense table stands outside the back door, you must not fail to come. If there is no incense table at the back door, you must on no account come.” The monk got out of bed and put on his headcloth as before. Ying'er opened the back door and let him out. From then on, whenever Yang Xiong went away to spend the night on prison duty, the monk came to the house. The old man always went to bed early, before evening had properly fallen, and the maid Ying'er had already joined their side. The only person they needed to deceive was Shi Xiu. Once the woman's lust was aroused, she cared for nothing else. The monk, too, had tasted the woman's charms, and the pair behaved as though their souls had been bewitched. The monk had only to wait until the mendicant gave the signal, and then he would leave the temple. The woman relied entirely on Ying'er as her go-between, letting the monk come and go, and thus took her pleasure by secretly keeping him as her lover. Their secret meetings continued in this way for more than a month. The monk came more than a dozen times.

p.src: Now Shi Xiu, after closing the shop each day, slept at the workshop. This matter constantly weighed on his mind, and day after day he remained uncertain, for he had never seen the monk coming or going. Each day around the fifth watch he would wake and now and then leap up, pondering the matter. He would hear the mendicant who announced the dawn come straight into the alley, beating his wooden fish and loudly invoking the Buddha. Shi Xiu was a sharp-witted man and had already guessed most of the truth. Privately he thought, “This alley is a dead end. Why has that mendicant come here day after day, beating his wooden fish and invoking the Buddha? There is something suspicious here. It was around the middle of the eleventh month. During the fifth watch, as Shi Xiu lay awake, he heard the wooden fish sounding. The mendicant beat it all the way into the alley and, on reaching the back door, cried loudly, “May all living beings be delivered! May those in suffering and peril be saved! All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!” Finding the cry peculiar, Shi Xiu sprang up and peered through a crack in the door. He saw a man wearing a headcloth slip out of the darkness and leave with the mendicant; immediately afterward, Ying'er came to shut the door. At the sight, Shi Xiu said to himself, “My brother is such a hero, yet grievously he has married this wanton woman. She has deceived him and carried on such a disgraceful affair behind his back.” He could scarcely wait for dawn. Then he carried the pork out before the shop and sold it at the morning market. After eating, he made a round collecting money owed on credit. Around noon, he went directly to the prefectural offices to find Yang Xiong. Just as he reached the prefectural bridge, he met Yang Xiong coming toward him. Yang Xiong asked, “Brother, where have you been?” Shi Xiu replied, “I was collecting some debts and came by to look for you.” Yang Xiong said, “Official duties always keep me busy, and I have never had the chance to enjoy a few cups with you. Come, let us sit here awhile.” Yang Xiong led Shi Xiu to a wineshop beneath the prefectural bridge. They chose a quiet private room and sat down, then called for the waiter to bring a jar of fine wine and prepare dishes, seafood, and drinking snacks. After they had drunk three cups, Yang Xiong saw that Shi Xiu merely kept his head lowered in thought. Yang Xiong was quick-tempered, and asked at once, “Brother, something seems to be troubling you. Has anyone at home said something to offend you?” Shi Xiu said, “No one at home has said anything. I am grateful that you treat me like your own flesh and blood. There is something I would like to say—may I speak?” Yang Xiong said, “Brother, why stand on ceremony with me today? If you have something to say, speak freely.” Shi Xiu said, “Each day when you go out, you attend only to your official duties, and know nothing of what happens behind your back. That sister-in-law of mine is no decent woman. I have seen the evidence several times, but until now I dared not speak. Today I saw everything clearly. Unable to contain myself, I came to find you. Please do not blame me for speaking plainly.” Yang Xiong said, “I have no one following me behind my back. Tell me—who is it?” Shi Xiu said, “When we held the Daoist service at home before, that thieving baldhead Preceptor Hai was invited. Sister-in-law exchanged amorous glances with him, and I saw it all. On the third day she went to the temple to fulfill her vow for the Blood-Bowl Repentance, and the two of them returned reeking of wine. Lately I have kept hearing a mendicant come straight into the alley, beating his wooden fish and invoking the Buddha. The fellow beats it in a most suspicious fashion. At the fifth watch today I rose and looked, and saw that it was indeed that thieving baldhead, wearing a headcloth as he came out of our house. What use is there in keeping such a wanton woman?” On hearing this, Yang Xiong flew into a rage. “How dare that wretched woman do such a thing!” Shi Xiu said, “Brother, calm your anger for now. Say nothing about it tonight, and behave just as you do every day. Tomorrow, merely pretend that you are going away for night duty, then return after the third watch and knock at the door. That fellow will certainly flee first through the back door. I shall seize him, and you may deal with him as you please.

p.src: At daybreak, Yang Xiong went downstairs and said to Old Pan, “Salt down the livestock already slaughtered. p.src: After taking his leave, Shi Xiu found an inn in a nearby lane, rented a room, and settled there. Shi Xiu pondered, “Yang Xiong and I swore brotherhood… If I do not get to the bottom of this matter, his life will be thrown away for nothing. p.src: That night he returned to the inn and slept until the fourth watch. Then, tucking his sharp self-defense dagger into his belt, he quietly opened the inn door and went straight to the lane behind Yang Xiong's house. He hid in the shadows and kept watch. Just as the fifth watch approached, he saw the mendicant monk coming to the mouth of the lane with his wooden fish tucked under his arm, peering furtively about. Shi Xiu darted behind him, seized the mendicant with one hand, and laid his blade against the man's neck with the other. In a low voice he growled, “Don't struggle. Raise your voice and I'll kill you. Just tell me the truth: what did Monk Hai send you here to do?” The mendicant said, “Good sir, spare me and I will tell you.” Shi Xiu said, “Speak quickly. I won't kill you.” The mendicant said, “Reverend Hai is having an affair with Pan's daughter and visits her every night. He ordered me to watch for an incense table by the back door as the signal, then summon him to go in; then during the fifth watch I am to come beating the wooden fish and invoking the Buddha, to summon him back out.” Shi Xiu asked, “Where is he now?” The mendicant replied, “He is still asleep in her house. Once I sound the wooden fish, he will come out.” Shi Xiu said, “Then lend me your clothes and wooden fish.” He stripped the clothes from the mendicant and took his wooden fish. As the mendicant was taking off his clothes, Shi Xiu drew the blade across his neck and killed him on the spot. Once the mendicant was dead, Shi Xiu put on his robe and leggings, tucked the dagger into his side, and went down the lane steadily beating the wooden fish. Lying in bed, Reverend Hai heard the wooden fish clacking and hurriedly rose, threw on his clothes, and came downstairs. Ying'er came first to open the door, and the monk slipped out behind her through the back entrance. Shi Xiu kept beating the wooden fish. The monk hissed softly, “Why do you keep beating that thing?” Shi Xiu made no answer. He let the monk reach the mouth of the lane, then tripped him, pinned him down, and barked, “Don't raise your voice! Shout, and I'll kill you. All I want is to strip off your clothes, and then we're done.” Reverend Hai recognized Shi Xiu and dared neither struggle nor make a sound. Shi Xiu stripped off every stitch of his clothing, leaving him stark naked. Then he quietly drew the blade from beside his knee and stabbed him three or four times, killing him. He placed the blade beside the mendicant's body, gathered up both men's clothes, rolled them into a bundle, and returned to the inn. Softly opening the door, he slipped inside, quietly closed it again, and went to sleep. Of that there is no more to tell. Now in that city there was an old man named Wang who sold rice cakes and gruel. Early that morning he set out for the morning market carrying his baskets of cakes and gruel, with a lantern lit and a young lad following behind. As he passed the spot where the corpses lay, he tripped over one of them and fell, spilling his whole load of cakes and gruel across the ground. The lad cried out, “What a disaster! A monk has passed out drunk here.” The old man felt his way back to his feet, only to find both hands smeared with blood. He cried out in distress, utterly bewildered. Several neighboring households heard the commotion and opened their doors to come out. When they shone their lights upon the scene, they saw blood and gruel spread everywhere and two corpses sprawled upon the ground. The neighbors seized the old man and dragged him away to report the matter to the authorities. Truly, misfortune fell from heaven and calamity sprang from the earth. How Old Wang ultimately escaped this predicament will be revealed in the next chapter.
